prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, reaching a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18 and opening new tests of fundamental physics

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks rest on a simple and original physical idea: at the magic wavelength the light shift of the two clock states cancels, so atoms can be held tightly in a standing wave, free of Doppler and recoil shifts, and a million of them can be interrogated at once. The result is a fractional uncertainty near 10^-18, which has made laboratory tests of gravitational redshift at the millimetre scale, searches for drifting constants and relativistic geodesy possible. This is also precisely the kind of close agreement between calculation and experiment that I trust: the magic wavelengths, the blackbody-radiation shift and the other systematic corrections depend on atomic-structure theory that has been checked repeatedly. The work has been reproduced and surpassed by independent laboratories in Japan, the USA, Germany, France, China and elsewhere, which compare their clocks over optical fibre, so this is not a single-experiment claim. Two names are a clean attribution: Katori for the magic-wavelength proposal and the first strontium lattice clock, Ye for taking the concept to record accuracy and stability and into many-body clock physics. I would not claim the prize rests on a single experiment, because it rests on a decade of agreement across laboratories.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is novelty. The 2005 prize (Hall and Hansch) gave the frequency comb that makes optical clocks countable, and the 2012 prize (Wineland, Haroche) honoured quantum control of single ions, which already set the accuracy record before lattice clocks did. A sceptic can say that lattice clocks are a major refinement of already recognised ideas and that their reach beyond metrology is still being demonstrated. The redefinition of the second has also not yet happened. Attribution is not entirely free of dispute either: Lemonde, Takamoto, Boyd and the PTB and NIST groups have real claims, and Ye's own work builds on comb and laser-stabilisation technology. Finally, a topological or tunable-matter discovery may reveal something more surprising about nature than a better clock does, which is a standard I normally apply myself.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first as a new way of measuring time, with many independent laboratories confirming it, but asks whether the committee sees the clock as a distinct instrument or as a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I share his ranking and I take the overlap question seriously. My answer is that the earlier prizes gave tools, the comb to count optical cycles and ion control for single-particle clocks, while the lattice clock solved a different problem, namely how to get both the statistics of many atoms and the freedom from motional shifts of a trapped one. That is a new physical idea, the magic wavelength, and not a refinement of the ion clock. I agree with him that the exact division of credit between the lattice concept and the later accuracy records is a judgement, and that is why I keep the citation tied to the invention and realization of the clock.

responses.point: Eriksson places the topological insulator candidate first, as a new quantum state of matter with robust edge transport, and places lattice clocks only sixth, noting overlap with the 2005 comb prize and ion-clock work.
responses.response: I agree that B008 is the strongest conceptual discovery on our list and I ranked it second myself. Where I disagree is the sixth place for the clocks. I do not think a measurement prize has to be justified by overlap alone: the lattice clock changed what can be measured, and its accuracy is now tested against independent clocks. I would also point out that his own attribution note admits that the BHZ prediction falls outside the credited names, so the topological configuration has a genuine allocation problem that the clock candidate does not have. If the committee prefers B008, I could support it with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, but I do not think it is cleaner on credit.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as the platform behind essentially all superconducting processors and argues that it is distinct from the 2025 prize on macroscopic tunnelling, while putting the lattice clock second.
responses.response: I respect that argument, and I ranked circuit QED third on the physics: strong coupling on a chip is real cavity QED. My reservation is the timing and the credit. A second superconducting-circuit prize a year after 2025 will look repetitive even if the discovery is distinct, and, as Johansson himself says, Girvin is missing from the trio and the proposal and experiment came from one Yale collaboration. I also hear in his note that part of the case rests on the platform's prospects for quantum computing, which is a technological motivation and not the strongest basis for this prize. I would be happy to revisit this in a later year.

responses.point: Danielsson places IceCube first as a genuine clue from nature that opened neutrino astronomy, while admitting that the source associations are still statistically moderate and that the collaboration size and AMANDA pioneers complicate a trio.
responses.response: This is a discovery of real consequence and I would not oppose it, and I ranked it fifth. I defer to him on the astroparticle judgement. The difficulty I see is that the prize would need to decide between honouring the detector builders and the diffuse-flux discovery, and a three-person split of a collaboration of hundreds, with AMANDA and Baikal pioneers outside the names, is less defensible than a two-person split for the clocks. I would ask him whether he would accept recognising the instrument concept and the 2013 flux detection alone, and leaving the source astronomy for later.

uncertainties: Whether the committee sees lattice clocks as a sufficiently new achievement after the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize.
Whether the contributions of Lemonde, Takamoto, Boyd and the PTB and NIST groups would force a wider allocation than Katori and Ye.
Whether the topological insulator candidate (B008), which has the broadest support, can be given a credit allocation that survives the missing BHZ names.
I have not independently verified specific record accuracy values and rely on my knowledge of the literature.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the candidates in my preferred configuration: I have no documented collaboration with Katori or Ye. I work in atomic structure theory, which is close to the physics of the magic wavelength, and I am a long-time collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate), but none of the shortlisted candidates involves her. I have no known connection to the other shortlisted candidates.
